badge.description: Displays a small label to highlight status, category, or metadata information in a compact visual format.
badge.overview: Badge is a compact visual indicator used to convey status, count, or categorical information. It renders as an inline element with customizable appearance through variant and color props. The component supports two variants: default with a solid background and outline with a bordered style. Nine color options are available including main, accent, success, error, info, warning, dark, light, and inherit. Badge can contain text, icons, or both, and supports the render prop for custom element rendering.
badge.usage: Use Badge to highlight important information such as status indicators, notification counts, or category labels. For basic usage, wrap text content inside the Badge component. Apply the variant prop to switch between solid and outline styles. Use the color prop to communicate semantic meaning such as success for positive states, error for alerts, or warning for caution. Combine with icons by including an Icon component as a child alongside text. For custom element rendering, pass a single element to the render prop.
badge.accessibility: This component meets the following accessibility requirements. For semantic structure, Badge renders as a span element by default, appropriate for inline content. When conveying status information, ensure surrounding context makes the meaning clear to screen readers. For focus states, the component includes visible focus indicators with a ring style meeting WCAG requirements. Color alone should not convey meaning, so pair colors with text labels or icons. When used with icons, ensure icons are either decorative or have appropriate aria-labels.

button.description: Triggers actions or events when clicked, supporting multiple visual styles and semantic colors.
button.overview: Button provides interactive elements for triggering actions in forms, dialogs, navigation, and other contexts. It supports three visual variants: default with solid background, outline with bordered style, and ghost with transparent background. Nine semantic colors are available including main, accent, success, error, warning, info, dark, light, and inherit. Four size options (default, sm, lg, icon) accommodate different layout needs. The render prop enables polymorphic rendering to wrap links or other elements while maintaining button styling.
button.usage: Use Button for primary actions, form submissions, and navigation triggers. For basic usage, render with children text and optional variant or color props. Apply outline variant for secondary actions and ghost variant for tertiary or subtle interactions. Use semantic colors to convey meaning: success for confirmations, error for destructive actions, warning for cautionary operations. The icon size creates circular buttons suitable for icon-only content. Use the render prop to render as anchor tags for navigation while preserving button appearance.
button.accessibility: This component meets the following accessibility requirements. For keyboard support, buttons are focusable via Tab and activated with Enter or Space keys. avatar.description: Displays a user or entity image with fallback support for missing or loading states.
avatar.overview: Avatar represents users, organizations, or entities in a compact visual format. It consists of three parts: Root container for layout, Image for displaying the profile picture, and Fallback for showing initials or placeholder content when the image is unavailable. dropdownMenu.description: Displays a list of actions or options in a floating panel triggered by a button or interactive element.
dropdownMenu.overview: DropdownMenu provides a compact way to present a set of actions, links, or options that appear when users interact with a trigger element. The component consists of two main parts: the trigger element that opens the menu and the menu content containing selectable items. Menu items support various content types including text, icons, and links. The floating panel automatically positions itself relative to the trigger and dismisses when users click outside or select an item.
dropdownMenu.usage: Use DropdownMenu for contextual actions, navigation shortcuts, user account menus, or settings access. For basic usage, wrap a trigger element with DropdownMenu.Trigger and render the menu items as DropdownMenu.Item nodes inside DropdownMenu.Popup, which is itself nested inside DropdownMenu.Positioner. DropdownMenu.Positioner owns the portal and floating-element positioning; DropdownMenu.Popup is the visible panel that carries the menu semantics, styling, and DOM/ARIA attributes. Each DropdownMenu.Item should wrap a link or button element for proper semantics. Customize alignment using the align prop with center, start, or end values on DropdownMenu.Positioner. Adjust spacing between the trigger and the panel using the sideOffset prop on DropdownMenu.Positioner. Combine icons with text labels for improved scannability. For mobile navigation, pair with a hamburger icon trigger. The menu supports both controlled and uncontrolled open states via the open and defaultOpen props.
dropdownMenu.accessibility: This component meets the following accessibility requirements. For keyboard support, the menu opens with Enter or Space on the trigger, navigates items with Arrow keys, selects with Enter, and closes with Escape. Regarding focus management, focus moves to the first menu item when opened and returns to the trigger when closed. Uses appropriate ARIA attributes including aria-expanded on the trigger and role menu on the content. Screen readers announce the menu state and item count. The modal prop controls whether background content remains interactive.

pagination.description: Provides pagination controls for navigating multi-page content with previous/next buttons and page numbers.
pagination.overview: Pagination provides an interface for navigating through large amounts of content split across multiple pages. It consists of a previous button, a list of page numbers, and a next button. When there are many pages, the usePagination hook automatically optimizes the displayed page numbers using ellipsis (...). Each page number is rendered as a Pagination.Item component, with the current page visually highlighted. The renderItem prop enables flexible customization of each page item.
pagination.usage: Use Pagination for navigating content divided into multiple pages such as blog post lists, search results, or data tables. For basic usage, specify the count prop for total pages and currentIndex prop for the current page number. Set click handlers via prevProps and nextProps, and define how each page number renders with the renderItem prop. The Pagination.Item component highlights the current page with the selected prop. When pages change, smoothly scroll content to the top of the page.
pagination.accessibility: This component meets the following accessibility requirements. For semantic HTML, the component renders as a nav element indicating it is pagination navigation. Regarding keyboard navigation, all page numbers and previous/next buttons are focusable via Tab and activated with Enter or Space keys. For disabled states, the previous button is automatically disabled on the first page and the next button on the last page. The current page is communicated to screen readers via appropriate ARIA attributes in addition to visual highlighting. Focus indicators are displayed with ring styles meeting WCAG requirements.

dontList: Use pagination for small item counts (less than 10 items)

form.description: Provides a structured container for form inputs with shared state management for labels, inputs, helper text, and validation states.
form.overview: Form is a compound component system that manages form field state through React Context. It consists of five sub-components: Control for state management, Label for field labels, Input for text input fields, Textarea for multi-line text input, and HelperText for supplementary information or error messages. The Control component provides shared state including error, disabled, required, and color theme that automatically propagates to all child components. This architecture ensures consistent styling and behavior across form elements without manual prop drilling.
form.usage: Use Form to create accessible form fields with consistent styling and state management. Wrap form elements with Form.Control to share state across Label, Input, Textarea, and HelperText components. For basic usage, nest Form.Label, Form.Input, and Form.HelperText within Form.Control. Apply the error prop to Form.Control to display error styling on all child elements simultaneously. Use the disabled prop to disable the entire form field group. The color prop switches between dark and light themes for different background contexts. For multi-line input, replace Form.Input with Form.Textarea. Input supports startAdornment and endAdornment props for icons or decorative elements.
form.accessibility: This component meets the following accessibility requirements. For semantic HTML, Form.Label renders as a native label element that should be associated with inputs using htmlFor and id attributes. Form.Input and Form.Textarea render as native input and textarea elements with proper disabled states. For error states, visual styling changes are accompanied by color contrast that meets WCAG 4.5:1 requirements. Screen readers can identify disabled fields through the native disabled attribute. Focus indicators are visible with ring styles that meet WCAG requirements. Helper text provides additional context that should be linked to inputs using aria-describedby for screen reader support.

scrollArea.description: Provides a scrollable container with styled scrollbars for overflow content management.
scrollArea.overview: ScrollArea creates a scrollable viewport for content that exceeds its container dimensions. The component consists of a root container that manages overflow behavior, a viewport that contains the scrollable content, and a scrollbar that appears when content overflows. By default, a vertical scrollbar is displayed, but you can configure horizontal scrollbars or custom scrollbars through the scrollbar prop. The scrollbar uses a semi-transparent thumb indicator that transitions smoothly on interaction. The viewport automatically inherits border-radius from its parent for consistent visual appearance.
scrollArea.usage: Use ScrollArea to contain content that may exceed available space such as lists, articles, code blocks, or any overflow content. For basic usage, wrap content inside the ScrollArea component and set height constraints via className prop. When the scrollbar prop is not specified, the component automatically displays a vertical scrollbar when content overflows the container boundaries. Customize the container appearance by passing Tailwind classes for padding, borders, and background styles. Combine with responsive height classes to adapt scroll areas to different viewport sizes. To enable horizontal scrolling, pass <ScrollArea.ScrollBar orientation="horizontal" /> to the scrollbar prop and ensure child content has a width greater than the container. To hide the scrollbar, set scrollbar={null}, though normally omitting the scrollbar prop will display the default vertical scrollbar.
scrollArea.accessibility: This component meets the following accessibility requirements. For keyboard support, the scroll area supports native keyboard scrolling with arrow keys, Page Up, Page Down, Home, and End keys when focused. Regarding focus management, the viewport element accepts a ref for programmatic focus control. Touch interaction is disabled on the scrollbar to prevent accidental scrolling on mobile devices, while the content area remains fully touch-scrollable. The component uses semantic overflow behavior that screen readers understand natively. Visible scrollbars provide clear indication of scrollable content without requiring hover interaction.

skeleton.description: Displays animated placeholder content while the actual content is loading, providing visual feedback to users.
skeleton.overview: Skeleton is a loading state component that shows placeholder shapes mimicking the layout of content being loaded. It consists of three sub-components: Line for text placeholders, Box for rectangular content areas like images, and Round for circular elements like avatars. For basic usage, wrap Skeleton.Line, Skeleton.Box, or Skeleton.Round components within the Skeleton root. Use Skeleton.Line for text content placeholders with customizable height via className. Use Skeleton.Box for image or card placeholders with optional centered icon. Use Skeleton.Round for avatar or circular element placeholders. Combine multiple sub-components to create layouts that match the expected content structure. Apply width constraints via className to match actual content dimensions.

popover.description: Displays rich content in a floating panel anchored to a trigger element for contextual information or interactions.
popover.overview: Popover presents contextual content in a floating panel that appears relative to a trigger element. It consists of a trigger that opens the popover, a content area for displaying information or interactive elements, and an optional close button. timeSeriesChart.description: Plots one or more series of values over time as lines, areas, or filled ranges, with reference lines and bands, a tooltip, a legend, and a period-aware time axis.
timeSeriesChart.overview: TimeSeriesChart answers the question of how a measurement changes over time. Each series is a list of timestamped points; the chart merges them onto a shared time axis, thins the tick labels to fit the selected period, and draws either lines or filled areas. Series colors come from the chart palette tokens in a fixed order that stays distinguishable for viewers with color vision deficiencies, and a series can opt into a status color to signal a threshold or condition. A null value leaves a gap instead of drawing a misleading connection, and the value axis fits the data so that small movements far from zero remain visible. Besides plain measurements, a series can be a band that carries a low and a high bound per timestamp and is drawn as a filled range, which is how a confidence interval, a percentile band, or the spread around a baseline is shown; stacking several bands of decreasing width behind one median line produces a fan chart. Separate from the series, thresholds draw a dashed horizontal line at a value with an optional label, and reference bands shade a value range across the full width. Both stretch the value axis when they fall outside the measured range, so a limit that has not been crossed stays visible. The curve between points is linear by default and can be set per chart or per series to a step for values that hold until they change, or to a smooth natural curve. The time axis and the tooltip read timestamps in a given IANA time zone, so a day of readings starts at local midnight rather than at UTC midnight.
timeSeriesChart.usage: Use TimeSeriesChart when the shape of a value over time matters: temperature across a month, portfolio value across a year, page views across a week. Pass a label that names the chart for assistive technology, a period that matches the span of the data so the axis ticks use a suitable format, and series whose labels are already localized. Use the area variant when the magnitude under the line is meaningful, and the line variant when only the trajectory matters. Add thresholds for the limits and targets the series is judged against, and bands for the range a value is expected to stay inside, giving each a status color that matches its meaning. Use a band series when the spread around a value is part of the measurement, and give the bounds and their median line the same color so they read as one series. Set timeZone to the IANA name of the zone the data belongs to, since the axis reads UTC otherwise. Keep interpolation linear for measurements, use step for values that hold until they change such as a thermostat setting, and reserve natural for decorative trends, because a smooth curve overshoots the points it passes through and can show a value crossing a limit that no measurement crossed. Provide a valueFormatter to attach units or currency formatting, and keep animation off unless the chart is the focus of an interaction. Pair every chart with a table view of the same numbers for readers who cannot use the visual.
timeSeriesChart.accessibility: The chart surface is focusable and exposes the chart label as its accessible name. Once focused, the left and right arrow keys step through the data points and update the tooltip, so keyboard users can read every value. Series are distinguished by a palette validated for color vision deficiencies, and the legend repeats each series label in text next to its swatch. Tooltips show the series label and formatted value in text. Threshold lines are dashed and carry an optional text label, so a limit is named rather than identified by its color. A band series repeats its label in the legend and reports both bounds in the tooltip as a range, so the spread is readable as numbers. Reference bands are drawn behind the data at a low opacity, which keeps the series above them at full contrast. The chart does not expose the underlying numbers to screen readers on its own; place a data table with the same values next to it for a complete alternative.

barChart.description: Compares values across categories as vertical bars, grouped or stacked for multiple series, with a tooltip and an optional legend.
barChart.overview: BarChart answers the question of how categories compare to each other at a point in time. Each series provides one value per category, and categories are drawn in the order given. With several series the bars are grouped side by side within each category so that both the per-category comparison and the per-series comparison stay readable. Setting stacked places those series on top of each other instead, giving one bar per category whose height is the total and whose segments are its parts; series stack in the order they are given, so the first series sits at the bottom and the legend reads in that same bottom to top order. Only the top segment carries rounded corners, because every other segment meets the one above it. A stack holds together only when every value is zero or greater, since a negative segment would cross the baseline. The value axis always starts at zero so bar lengths are proportional to the values, and series colors follow the same palette order as the time series chart.
barChart.usage: Use BarChart when the reader needs to compare discrete categories: spending by category, allocation by asset class, energy by day of the week. Pass a label that names the chart for assistive technology, the categories already localized and in the order they should appear, and one series per measurement with one value per category. Set stacked when the category total is meaningful and the series are parts of it, such as sleep stages that add up to one night, and keep the grouped layout when the series are compared against each other rather than summed. Provide a valueFormatter to attach units or currency formatting. Keep the number of categories small enough that labels remain readable, and pair the chart with a table view of the same values.
barChart.accessibility: The chart surface is focusable and exposes the chart label as its accessible name. Once focused, the left and right arrow keys move between categories and update the tooltip, so keyboard users can read every value. Category labels are rendered as text on the axis, the legend repeats each series label in text next to its swatch, and the tooltip lists the series label and formatted value for the active category. In a stacked chart the tooltip lists every segment of the active category in stack order, which matches the order of the legend, so a segment is identified by position as well as by color. The chart does not expose the underlying numbers to screen readers on its own; place a data table with the same values next to it for a complete alternative.

statTile.description: Presents one headline number with its label, an optional change badge with a trend arrow, a short supporting line, and an optional compact chart.
statTile.overview: StatTile is the hero-number pattern for dashboards: values whose job is to state a single current magnitude rather than a shape over time. A small label sits above a large tabular-figure value, an optional delta badge whose arrow shows whether the value moved up, down, or stayed flat sits in the top-right corner, and an optional description such as the comparison period follows beneath the value. An optional chart slot holds one compact visualization, such as a Sparkline, pinned to the bottom edge so a row of tiles keeps a common baseline. The slot accepts any element and renders nothing for a value that is not one, so a tile without a chart keeps its layout instead of reserving empty space. The tile owns only layout and emphasis; the value and the delta text arrive already formatted so the app keeps full control over units, currency, and locale.
statTile.usage: Use StatTile for the key figures at the top of a dashboard page, typically in a row of two to four tiles: total portfolio value, period return, dividends received, overall yield. Pass a short label that names the measurement, the formatted value, and a delta whose label includes its sign so the direction is readable as text. The delta chip is tinted by direction, up as positive and down as negative; when a falling number is good news, such as a drop in expenses, set the delta sentiment to positive so the color matches the meaning. Reserve the description for context the reader needs to interpret the number, such as the comparison period. Put a Sparkline in the chart slot when the recent shape of the number helps read it, and give that sparkline its own label, because the tile label does not describe it. When the question is how a value changed over time or how categories compare, use a chart beside the tiles instead.
statTile.accessibility: The label, value, delta text, and description are all rendered as plain text in reading order, so screen readers announce the tile as a short sentence. The trend arrow is decorative and hidden from assistive technology; the direction must be carried by the delta text itself, for example with a leading plus or minus sign. The delta chip keeps its text in the default ink color and conveys sentiment only through its tint and icon, so the chip meets contrast requirements while never relying on color alone. A visualization placed in the chart slot carries its own accessible name, which the tile neither supplies nor overrides. The tile has no interactive parts of its own.

Format the value and the delta in the consuming app, including units and sign
Use the description for the comparison period or data source
Put one compact visualization such as a Sparkline in the chart slot
Group related tiles in a single row with consistent spacing
Pair the tiles with the charts and tables that explain them

Leave a sparkline in the chart slot without its own label
Rely on the arrow alone to communicate direction without a sign in the text
Use the delta badge for unrelated status text

table.description: Composable table parts for hand-built tables: header, body, footer, rows, heading cells, data cells, and a caption that share one set of rules and spacing.
table.overview: Table is the primitive under every table in the library. Table itself renders the table element inside a container that scrolls horizontally when columns overflow, and its parts map one to one onto the native elements: Table.Header, Table.Body, and Table.Footer are the row groups, Table.Row is a row, Table.Head is a heading cell, Table.Cell is a data cell, and Table.Caption is the caption. Rows are separated by one pixel rules, the last body row has none, a row highlights while hovered, and a row marked with the selected state keeps a tint. Every part accepts a class name so a consumer can right-align numbers, fix column widths, or wrap the whole table in a bordered frame.
table.usage: Compose the parts directly when the table is written by hand, such as an invoice list with a total row, or when a table needs column widths, spans, or cell content that the data-driven DataTable does not express. Right-align numeric cells with text-right and tabular figures so digits line up, put summary rows in Table.Footer, and wrap the table in a rounded bordered frame when it should read as a card. Reach for DataTable instead when columns and rows come from data and a caption is all the table needs.
table.accessibility: Every part renders its native element, so assistive technology announces the table with its caption as the name, the row and column counts, and each cell with its column heading. Put scope col on heading cells so the association is explicit. A visually hidden caption still names the table, and a table without a caption needs an aria-label. The hover and selected tints convey no state on their own; a consumer that selects rows must also expose the selection through aria-selected or a control inside the row.

Set scope col on every Table.Head
Right-align numbers with text-right and tabular figures
Keep summary rows in Table.Footer
Use DataTable when the rows come straight from data

dataTable.description: Renders tabular data as a semantic table with a caption, column headers, and right-aligned numeric columns.
dataTable.overview: DataTable is the text view of dashboard data: the same numbers that charts draw, laid out as rows and columns that every reader and assistive technology can traverse. It composes the Table parts inside a rounded bordered frame. Columns declare their heading and whether they hold numbers, rows map column ids to cell content, and an optional empty message fills one full-width row when there are no rows. The table always carries a caption that names it, which can be visually hidden when a heading above the table already does that job. Sorting, pagination, and selection are intentionally out of scope.
dataTable.usage: Use DataTable next to every chart on a page so that the underlying values are available as text, and on their own for lists that are naturally tabular such as allocation by asset class or transactions in a period. Provide a caption that says what the table contains and for which period, localize headers and cell content in the consuming app, mark numeric columns with align end so their digits line up, and pass an empty message so an empty period explains itself instead of showing a bare header. Keep the number of columns small enough to read without horizontal scrolling on common screens; the container scrolls horizontally only as a fallback.
dataTable.accessibility: The component renders a native table with a caption, so assistive technology announces the table name, row and column counts, and each cell with its column header. Column headers are marked with the column scope. The caption remains in the accessibility tree when it is visually hidden. Numeric columns use tabular figures and right alignment for scanning. Rows highlight while hovered to aid scanning; the highlight conveys no state, and the table has no interactive parts of its own.

periodSelector.description: Steps through periods with previous and next buttons around a label naming the current period.
periodSelector.overview: PeriodSelector is the control for choosing which month, quarter, or year a dashboard page shows. It shows the current period as text between two icon buttons for stepping backwards and forwards. donutChart.description: Shows how one total divides into parts as a ring, with an optional headline in the hole, a tooltip, and a legend.
donutChart.overview: DonutChart answers the question of how a whole splits into parts at one point in time. Each slice carries an id, a localized label, and a value, and the ring is drawn in the order the slices are given with a thin separator between neighbours. The hole holds an optional headline value and caption, rendered as selectable text rather than as part of the drawing, so the total reads as text while the slices underneath still answer the pointer. Slice colors come from the chart palette tokens in a fixed order that stays distinguishable for viewers with color vision deficiencies, and a slice can opt into a status color. The tooltip reports the formatted value together with its share of the total as a whole percentage.
donutChart.usage: Use DonutChart when the composition of a single total is the point: asset allocation by instrument, spending by category, storage by file type. Pass a label that names the chart for assistive technology and slices whose labels are already localized. Supply centerValue and centerLabel to state the total that the ring divides, and a valueFormatter to attach units or currency formatting. Keep the slice count at five or fewer and group the remainder into one other slice, because thin slices are hard to compare by angle. Slices answer the pointer rather than the keyboard, so the tooltip cannot be reached without a mouse or touch, which makes a data table with the same values required next to the chart rather than optional. The legend repeats each slice label in text next to its swatch, so slices are identified without relying on color. The center text sits in the reading order as real text, so screen readers announce the headline and its caption. Neighbouring slices are separated by a stroke in the surface color, which keeps their boundary visible when two palette colors sit next to each other.

scatterChart.description: Plots pairs of measurements as points on two numeric axes, with an optional fitted trend line, a tooltip, and a legend.
scatterChart.overview: ScatterChart answers the question of whether two measurements move together. Each series is a list of x and y pairs, both axes are numeric and fit their domain to the data, and the grid rules run in both directions because both measures carry meaning. An optional trend line is drawn as a dashed line across the measured horizontal range, so it stops where the data stops instead of running to the edge of the axis. Its slope and intercept are supplied by the consuming app, which keeps the drawn line identical to the fit the data source reports. Series colors follow the chart palette order, and the tooltip names the series and lists both measures with their own labels and formatting.
scatterChart.usage: Use ScatterChart when the relationship between two measurements matters: carbon dioxide against sleep quality, outdoor temperature against energy use, price against yield. Pass a label for assistive technology, xLabel and yLabel that name the two measures, and one series per group of observations. Provide xValueFormatter and yValueFormatter so each axis carries its own unit. Add a trendLine only when the fit comes from the plotted data, and name the method in the surrounding text. The tooltip labels both numbers with xLabel and yLabel, so a reading is never left to axis position alone. The trend line is dashed rather than solid, so it stays distinct from a series without relying on color.

sankeyChart.description: Traces how a quantity moves between stages as ribbons whose width is the amount, with a tooltip for every flow and node.
sankeyChart.overview: SankeyChart answers the question of where a quantity goes as it passes through stages. Nodes name the places a quantity rests, links carry an amount from one node to another, and the layout places nodes in columns and draws each link as a ribbon whose thickness is proportional to its value. Node labels sit beside their column and turn inward on the right-hand side, so the last column stays inside the surface. Node colors follow the chart palette order while the ribbons stay a neutral tint, which keeps the nodes as the emphasis. Hovering a ribbon reports the flow from source to target with its value, and hovering a node reports that node total.
sankeyChart.usage: Use SankeyChart when the movement of an amount between stages is the point: income divided into spending and savings, energy from source to use, visitors from channel to outcome. Keep the graph shallow, at two or three columns, and keep node counts low so the ribbons stay traceable. A link whose source or target is missing from the node list is dropped rather than drawn, so validate ids in the consuming app instead of relying on that fallback. Give the chart a generous height, because ribbons and their labels need vertical room.

calendarHeatmap.description: Lays out daily values as a grid of small squares, one column per week, shaded on a four-step color scale.
calendarHeatmap.overview: CalendarHeatmap answers the question of which days a measurement ran high and how regularly that happened. Days fill a grid of seven rows starting at Monday, one column per week, and the range is padded outward to whole weeks so the grid stays rectangular. A day the data omits and a day whose value is null both render as an outlined empty cell, which stays distinct from a measured zero. Values map to four opaque steps of the chosen palette color, mixed toward the surface color rather than made translucent, so the contrast of every step is fixed and verifiable. The scale runs from zero to the largest value unless max is set, which is what makes two grids comparable. Optional weekday labels sit on every other row so they do not collide at the small cell size, and an optional legend names the low and high ends of the scale.
calendarHeatmap.usage: Use CalendarHeatmap for a long run of daily values where the pattern across weeks matters more than the exact number: steps per day, days with a workout, entries per day. Pass a label that names the measurement and its span, and days as ISO calendar dates with their values. Treat each date as an opaque calendar day already resolved in the consuming app, because the grid never shifts a date between time zones. Set max explicitly when several grids are compared, so their scales agree. Pass weekdayLabels and scaleLabels already localized, and a valueFormatter so the per-cell hover text carries units. Choose MatrixHeatmap when the two dimensions are something other than weeks and weekdays.
calendarHeatmap.accessibility: The grid is exposed as a single image with the chart label as its accessible name, so assistive technology announces what the grid shows instead of reading hundreds of cells. Each measured cell carries its date and formatted value as native hover text, which the pointer reaches but the keyboard does not, so a table of the same values is required for a complete alternative. The four color steps are opaque, so their contrast against the surface does not depend on what sits behind them. Missing days are drawn as outlined cells rather than as a paler shade, so absence is not read as a low value. The legend names the low and high ends in words instead of leaving the ramp to be inferred.

matrixHeatmap.description: Shades a grid of values across two named dimensions, with row and column headings and an optional scale legend.
matrixHeatmap.overview: MatrixHeatmap answers the question of where two dimensions intersect at high values. Rows and columns are named by the consuming app, and values arrive as a grid indexed by row and then by column. Each cell is a square shaded on the same four opaque steps as the calendar grid, mixed toward the surface color so the contrast of every step is fixed. A value at or below min renders as the empty step and a null renders as an outlined cell, which keeps a missing reading distinct from a low one. The scale spans min to max, and both can be set so several grids share one scale. Row headings sit to the left of each row and column headings above the grid, both as plain text.
matrixHeatmap.usage: Use MatrixHeatmap when a measurement is indexed by two named dimensions: hour of day against day of week, room against month, channel against campaign. Pass a label that names the measurement and its span, localized row and column headings, and a values grid whose rows align with the row headings. Set min and max when the meaningful range does not start at zero, such as carbon dioxide that never falls below the outdoor level, since without min the empty step marks only an exact zero. Provide a valueFormatter so the per-cell hover text carries units, and keep the grid small enough that headings stay readable. Choose CalendarHeatmap when the two dimensions are weeks and weekdays.
matrixHeatmap.accessibility: The grid is exposed as a single image with the chart label as its accessible name, so assistive technology announces what the grid shows instead of reading every cell. Row and column headings are rendered as text, so a cell can be located without reading the shading. Each measured cell carries its headings and formatted value as native hover text, which the pointer reaches but the keyboard does not, so a table of the same values is required for a complete alternative. The four color steps are opaque, so their contrast against the surface does not depend on what sits behind them. Missing readings are drawn as outlined cells rather than as a paler shade, so absence is not read as a low value.

Localize row and column headings in the consuming app
Align every values row with its row heading
Set min and max when the meaningful range does not start at zero
Pass null for a reading that is missing
Provide a table view of the same values
dontList: Fill missing readings with zero to keep the grid full
Mix measurements with different units in one grid
Crowd the grid with more headings than can be read
Pass raw colors or CSS values instead of the chart palette
Rely on the hover text, which the keyboard cannot reach
Read exact values off the shading

sparkline.description: Draws a bare trend line for a short run of values, sized to fit inside a tile or a table cell.
sparkline.overview: Sparkline answers the question of which way a number has been moving, in about the space of a line of text. It draws the values as a single stroke with no axes, ticks, grid, or tooltip, scaled so the smallest value sits at the bottom of the box and the largest at the top. Because the scale comes from the values themselves, the line shows shape rather than magnitude, and a run of identical values sits flat in the middle. A null breaks the stroke instead of interpolating across it, so the values are drawn as separate runs, and a lone measurement between gaps renders as a dot. The stroke keeps its weight when the box is stretched, so the same values read consistently in a wide tile and in a narrow cell.
sparkline.usage: Use Sparkline next to a number that already states the magnitude: inside a StatTile, in a trend column of a DataTable, or beside a heading. Pass a label that names the measurement and its span, because the line carries no axis to read it from. Set the size with className, since the drawing stretches to whatever box it is given. Pass null for a gap rather than dropping the point, so the spacing between measurements stays even. Choose a chart palette color that matches the series the line belongs to. Choose TimeSeriesChart when the reader needs to read values, dates, or a scale from the chart.
sparkline.accessibility: The drawing is exposed as a single image with the label as its accessible name, so assistive technology announces what the line shows instead of describing a shape. The component has no interactive parts and no tooltip, so nothing is reachable by pointer alone. The exact values must be available as text nearby, in the tile value, the table cell, or a table view. The stroke is the only carrier of the information, so it stays on a chart palette color against the surface rather than being tinted for decoration. A break in the line is a gap in the data, not a visual style.
doList: Give every sparkline a label that names the measurement and its span
Place it next to the number it supports
Set the width and height with className
Pass null for a missing value to keep the spacing even
Use a chart palette color that matches the series
dontList: Use it as the only view of a value
Read magnitude from it, since the scale fits the values
Drop missing points instead of passing null
Stretch it wide enough that a full chart would fit
Add axis labels or a legend around it

hypnogram.description: Shows one sleep session as stage segments on a time axis, with a row per stage from awake at the top to deep at the bottom.
hypnogram.overview: Hypnogram answers the question of how a sleep session moved between stages. Each segment carries a start, an end, and one of four stages: awake, REM, core, and deep. Rows run from the lightest stage at the top to the deepest at the bottom, and every segment is drawn as a bar on its own row with a thin connector to the segment before it, so the descent into deep sleep and the return toward waking read as one path. Segments are sorted by start, and the chart spans the first start to the last end. The time axis labels both ends plus the whole hours between them, read on the wall clock of the given time zone. Stage colors come from the palette with one default per stage, and each default can be overridden.
hypnogram.usage: Use Hypnogram for a single sleep session, or for another sequence of a few named states across hours. Pass a label that names the session and its span, segments in epoch milliseconds where each end is the next start, and stageLabels already localized. Set timeZone to the IANA name of the zone the session was slept in, so the hour labels read as the local clock, since the labels read in UTC otherwise. Override stageColors only to match a palette the reader already knows. Put the time spent in each stage next to the chart as text or a table, because durations are hard to add up by eye. Choose BarChart to compare stage totals across several nights.
hypnogram.accessibility: The drawing is exposed as a single image with the label as its accessible name, so assistive technology announces the session instead of reading every segment. Stage names are rendered as text at the start of each row, so a row is identified without relying on its color. Rows run from the lightest stage to the deepest, so depth is carried by position as well as by color. The chart has no tooltip and no interactive parts, so no information is reachable by pointer alone. Time labels use a 24 hour clock in the given zone, which keeps a session that crosses midnight unambiguous.

Provide the time spent in each stage as text or a table

Leave gaps between segments that the axis cannot explain

concept_description: B.G. Neo Grid Design System is a design foundation that steadily advances toward the future while retaining the warmth of a sunlit, tranquil room. Within a comfortable retro environment, it establishes a platform that connects the present with what comes next by combining functionality and scalability designed for the coming era. It is a new design framework that blends the refined structure of a near-future metropolis with the lived-in retro vintage charm of the 80s and 90s. Reminiscent of a modest retro apartment room adorned with well-worn tin decor and indoor plant greenery, it conveys a modern outline that looks confidently toward the future.

introduction.title: B.G. Neo Grid Design System

items.heading: The Warmth of a Futuristic Metropolis
items.text: Combines the sleek feeling of a futuristic urban environment with the cozy warmth of materials such as wood and tin. It incorporates the familiar atmosphere of everyday furniture and interiors into a grid layout, creating a gentle and welcoming ambiance that isn't too sterile.

items.heading: A Retro Space Illuminated by Warm Light
items.text: Utilizes retro furniture and decor with a tone and manner centered on bright light. Indoor plants, soft wood hues, and subtle metal accents balance retro charm and sophistication.

items.heading: A Simple Grid Structure Resembling Pixel Art
items.text: Designed such that small components gather to form a grid that drives overall growth, akin to pixels forming pixel art; the combination of discrete parts creates meaning and value.

items.heading: Harmony Between Nature and Industrial
items.text: Integrates industrial elements like tin storage and steel shelving with natural materials and greenery to achieve a perfect balance of softness. The combination of urban, hard elements with a soothing, home-like atmosphere creates a unique interior aesthetic.

introduction.itemAlt: An abstract image representing the composition of component data.

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.intro: B.G. Neo Grid Design System strives for comfort and functionality. We focus on the following points to deliver a unique world that fuses futuristic flair with a retro material aesthetic to all users.
accessibility.imageAlt: An illustration representing the composition of component data.

items.title: Web Accessibility and WCAG Compliance
paragraphs: Aim to achieve WCAG 2.1 AA or higher while incorporating retro design, ensuring proper contrast, structure, and ease of navigation.
Implement machine-readable code, appropriate semantics, and focus management as the baseline, integrating accessibility requirements into UI component design.

items.title: Color and Contrast
paragraphs: Adopt an approach where small elements combine to form the whole, assessing and improving accessibility on a component-by-component basis.
Continuously update to meet accessibility standards even as new features and design elements are introduced.

items.title: Text and Typography
paragraphs: While using near-futuristic and industrial elements, incorporate natural touches like wood textures or greenery to evoke warmth.
Ensure that warm color palettes and textures do not compromise legibility by strictly maintaining appropriate contrast ratios and color accessibility.

items.title: Interaction and Navigation
paragraphs: Incorporate design nuances reminiscent of retro decor and vintage furniture, complemented by brightness and soft saturation reminiscent of daylight.
Even with soft hues, ensure that text and icons remain legible through optimal contrast and color schemes.

items.heading: Basic Requirements
items.paragraph: Meet essential standards such as text/background contrast, font sizes, line spacing, etc. Ensure interactive elements are clearly visible with a minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1.

items.heading: Screen Reader Support
items.paragraph: Structure HTML appropriately so that assistive technologies can accurately read content. Decorative images should have empty alt attributes, while informative images must have appropriate alt text.

items.heading: Keyboard Navigation
items.paragraph: Ensure all interactive elements (forms, buttons, links, modals, etc.) can be operated via keyboard. Set logical tab order and provide skip links to main content.

items.heading: Alternative Text for Images
items.paragraph: Exclude decorative images from screen reader narration and assign appropriate alt text to UI elements with functional images.

items.heading: Video and Audio
items.paragraph: Provide captions for videos and textual descriptions. Avoid autoplay for audio, and offer easy controls for volume adjustment and pausing.

items.heading: Forms
items.paragraph: Display clear labels for input fields, and communicate required fields and errors effectively. Implementations should accurately inform screen readers of any error messages.

items.heading: Layout Structure
items.paragraph: Organize information in a clear and logical hierarchy and ensure that the layout is user-friendly on mobile devices.

items.heading: Color Usage
items.paragraph: Set appropriate contrast between text and background, and consider diverse color perceptions for effective communication.

items.heading: Clear Writing
items.paragraph: Use simple language and clearly describe interactive processes. Maintain proper heading hierarchy and organize content effectively.

items.heading: Animation
items.paragraph: Use animations sparingly and provide options to pause when necessary. Avoid overly aggressive or flashing animations.

items.heading: Layout
items.paragraph: Structure header, main content, and footer appropriately to ensure mobile responsiveness and usability.

items.heading: Modal Dialogs
items.paragraph: When displaying modals, dim the background and manage focus appropriately with consideration for screen reader use.

items.heading: Notifications
items.paragraph: Ensure notifications are clearly visible and accurately communicated to screen readers.

items.heading: Slideshows
items.paragraph: Provide options to pause autoplay and allow manual control, ensuring that the current slide content is effectively conveyed to screen readers.

items.heading: Tooltips
items.paragraph: Clearly control the display of additional information to ensure that its visibility and hiding are well-managed for screen readers.

items.heading: Sorting Functionality
items.paragraph: Allow sorting to be operated via both mouse and keyboard, with clear indication of actionable areas and outcomes.

items.heading: Menus
items.paragraph: For mobile menus, provide appropriate labels and clearly indicate open or closed states.

items.heading: Page Transitions
items.paragraph: Always display the current location and clearly indicate the purpose of links and buttons. Notify users appropriately when the page content is updated.

responsive.title: Responsive

description.paragraph1: We aim to provide a UI that is comfortable across various screen sizes, offering a modern yet approachable design. The goal is to deliver a user-friendly and warm UI experience even on the latest devices, while always keeping accessibility (WCAG 2.1 AA and above) in mind as layouts adapt fluidly based on screen size.
description.paragraph2: Each component is designed to flexibly expand or contract according to screen size, maintaining a basic layout that facilitates easy element arrangement. Even on small screens, careful color usage and appropriate spacing ensure that the main content remains clear and readable.

responsive.heroImageAlt: An abstract image representing the data structure of a component

breakpoints.heading: Breakpoints
breakpoints.description: This design system sets key breakpoints based on screen size. On smaller screens, fewer elements are displayed per row with a vertical layout; on larger screens, multi-column layouts are utilized for a cohesive design.

row2.usage: Optimized for small tablets or large smartphones

row3.usage: For landscape tablets or small PCs

row4.usage: Suitable for laptops and typical desktops

row5.usage: For large desktops or TV displays

item1.heading: Design Consistency and Accessibility
paragraphs: On small screens, tactile colors and icons evoke a warm design; elements are appropriately omitted or rearranged to maintain overall consistency.

When view switching or wrapping occurs, careful considerations ensure that text size and tap targets do not become excessively small, and that focus movement or reading order remains intact during media query-triggered layout changes.

item2.heading: Grid System Design
paragraphs: For Small screens, a 4-column grid is used for simplicity; for Medium screens, a 6-column layout is employed; and for Large screens and beyond, a 12-column grid increases layout flexibility.

On smaller screens, sufficient spacing is maintained to prevent clutter while ensuring a minimum tap target size (approximately 44px square), and on larger screens, generous margins enhance visual clarity.
The layout is organized in a left-to-right reading order, with major elements such as hero images or cards spanning columns for impactful display.

item3.heading: Navigation Implementation
paragraphs: On Small screens, the global navigation is contained within a hamburger menu, with appropriate aria-labels and aria-expanded attributes ensuring accessibility.
On Medium screens and above, navigation items are displayed in a header or fixed sidebar, combining icons with text to ensure clear visibility.

item4.heading: Images and Decorative Elements
paragraphs: On small screens, decorative background images are managed so as not to obscure text, and decorative illustrations are provided with empty alt attributes.
Appropriate images are provided based on screen size, and decorative elements are carefully arranged to avoid interfering with UI components.
An overlay is used behind images to maintain proper contrast and accessibility.

item5.heading: Typography and Form Elements
paragraphs: Text size adjusts responsively, with automatic modifications to line spacing and letter spacing.
When using background colors, a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 is maintained, with careful consideration for text wrapping on small screens.
Forms are designed to adapt their layout based on screen size, with clear and accessible error messages.

item6.heading: Component Implementation Points
paragraphs: Components such as carousels, modals, and notifications are designed with responsive display in mind, ensuring accessibility at all times.
Optimized media queries, refined animations, considerations for both touch and mouse interactions, and proper management of aria attributes all contribute to a UI catered to every user.
